---
title: "Write Text"
subtitle: "Headings, emphasis, links, and the boxes that make a page easy to read"
---

::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Write and format text in Visual mode, and read the same text in Source mode
- Structure a page with headings that work for navigation and screen readers
- Use callouts, tabs, key-point boxes and footnotes in the right places
- Link to other chapters and to the glossary
:::

## Two views of the same file

Every chapter is a text file. RStudio shows it in one of two ways, switched by
the **Source** and **Visual** buttons at the top-left of the editor.

- **Visual** looks like a word processor. Use the toolbar for bold, lists and
  links, and the **Insert** menu for pictures, tables, callouts and more.
- **Source** shows the plain text, with a few symbols marking the formatting.
  This is called *markdown*.

You can switch at any time without losing anything. If you never want to see
markdown, you never have to. But it is worth being able to *read* it, because
this course shows examples in that form, and because a fix in Source view is
sometimes faster than hunting for the right menu.

## Markdown in one table

The left column is what you type in Source view. The right column is what the
reader sees.

| You type | The reader sees |
|---|---|
| `## A heading` | (a section heading, see below) |
| `**important**` | **important** |
| `*emphasis*` | *emphasis* |
| `` `file.qmd` `` | `file.qmd` |
| `- item` on a new line | a bullet point |
| `1. step` on a new line | a numbered step |
| `[the glossary](glossary.qmd)` | [the glossary](glossary.qmd) |
| `> quotation` | a quotation block |
: The handful of markdown symbols you will use daily {#tbl-markdown}

A blank line separates paragraphs. A list needs a blank line before it. That is
nearly all there is.

## The top of every file

Each chapter starts with a small block between two lines of three dashes:

```markdown
---
title: "Write Text"
subtitle: "Headings, emphasis, links, and the boxes that make a page easy to read"
---
```

The `title` becomes the page heading and the entry in the sidebar. The `subtitle`
is optional and appears underneath. Keep the quotation marks and the dashes.

## Headings

Use headings to divide the chapter into short sections. In Source view they are
lines starting with `##` (a main section) or `###` (a subsection):

```markdown
## Main section

### A subsection inside it
```

In Visual mode, use the paragraph-style drop-down in the toolbar and choose
*Heading 2* or *Heading 3*.

Three rules, because headings do more work than they appear to:

1. **Do not use `#` (a single hash) inside a chapter.** The page title already
   uses that level. Start with `##`.
2. **Never skip a level.** A `###` belongs under a `##`.
3. **Never fake a heading with bold text.** Real headings feed the "On this page"
   list on the right, the automatic numbering, and search. They are also how
   people using a screen reader jump around the page. Bold text does none of
   that.

::: {.keypoint}
**Key point**

A learner scans before they read. Make the headings tell the story on their own:
"How to add a chapter" beats "Chapters".
:::

## Writing for the screen

Reading on a screen is not reading on paper. A few habits help:

- **Short paragraphs**, three or four sentences.
- **Say the point first**, then explain.
- **Link text should make sense alone.** "Read the [glossary](glossary.qmd)" is
  good; "click [here](glossary.qmd)" is not, because screen-reader users often
  hear a list of links with no surrounding text.
- **Use lists** when items are parallel, and **numbered lists** only when order
  matters.
- Write in the second person ("you will") and keep sentences plain.

## Linking

To link to another chapter, use its file name, not a web address:

```markdown
See [Chapter 2](02-plan-and-structure.qmd) for how to add a chapter.
```

This keeps working after the course is published, even if the web address
changes. To link to another website, use the full address starting with
`https://`. In Visual mode, select the words and press *Ctrl+K* (*Cmd+K* on a
Mac).

## Boxes that carry meaning

Boxes draw the eye, so each kind should mean one thing, and a page should have
few of them. This template has two families.

### Callouts

Callouts are built in. There are five kinds; the colour and icon follow the
university's palette.

::: {.callout-note}
## Note

Extra information that is useful but not essential.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Tip

A shortcut or a piece of good practice.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Important

Something the reader must not miss.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Warning

A step where mistakes are likely or costly.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Caution

Something that can cause a problem in specific circumstances.
:::

In Source view a callout is written like this. The words after `callout-` pick the
kind, and the `##` line is its title:

```markdown
::: {.callout-warning}
## Warning

A step where mistakes are likely or costly.
:::
```

In Visual mode, use **Insert → Callout**. Add `collapse="true"` inside the braces
to make a callout start folded, which is useful for extra detail:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Click to unfold: an optional detail

Folded callouts keep the main path short. Learners who want the detail can open
it; the rest can skip it.
:::

### Objectives and key point

Two boxes are specific to this template. Both are made the same way, with a
`::: {.name}` line, their content, and a closing `:::`. In Visual mode use
**Insert → Div…** and type the class name (`objectives` or `keypoint`) into the
attributes field.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Objectives

Once, at the top of a chapter, in blue.

```markdown
::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Write objectives that can be checked
- Cut a topic into chapters
:::
```

## Key point

Once per section at most, in yellow. The one thing to remember.

```markdown
::: {.keypoint}
**Key point**

You edit the text files, never the finished website.
:::
```

:::

Tabs, as you just used, are also useful for alternatives such as "Windows" and
"Mac". Each `##` heading inside a `::: {.panel-tabset}` block becomes a tab.

## Footnotes

A footnote gives a side remark without breaking the flow.[^first] Type `^[your
note here]` right where the note belongs, or use **Insert → Footnote** in Visual
mode. On a computer, hovering over the number shows the note.

[^first]: Like this one. It appears at the bottom of the page, and pops up when
you hover over the number.

## Explaining terms

Every field has words that learners do not know yet. Put them in the glossary
page (`glossary.qmd`), and mark the first use in the text so that hovering shows
the meaning. For example, the word [render]{.gloss title="Build the website from the text files"}
below has a dotted underline: on a computer, hover to see the explanation.

```markdown
Click [render]{.gloss title="Build the website from the text files"} again.
```

Hover text does not appear on touch screens, so the glossary page is the primary
place for definitions. The hover is a convenience.

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz-score}
:::

::: {.question}
You want to start a new section in the middle of a chapter. What do you type?

- [ ] `# New section`
- [x] `## New section`
- [ ] `**New section**`
- [ ] `NEW SECTION`

::: {.feedback}
`##` makes a real heading, one level below the page title. A single `#` is
reserved for the title, and bold text is not a heading at all, so it would not
appear in the "On this page" list.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
Which link text is best?

- [ ] Click [here](glossary.qmd) for the glossary
- [ ] [https://…/glossary.html](glossary.qmd)
- [x] Look up the term in the [glossary](glossary.qmd)
- [ ] [Link](glossary.qmd)

::: {.feedback}
Good link text describes the destination and makes sense when read on its own,
which is how screen-reader users often meet links.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
For a warning that only some readers need to see, in full detail, you should use:

- [ ] A key-point box
- [x] A callout with `collapse="true"`
- [ ] A heading
- [ ] Red text

::: {.feedback}
A folded callout keeps the main text short and leaves the detail to whoever wants
it. Red text is not part of the template's palette, and colour alone should never
carry the meaning anyway.
:::
:::

The symbol pair you type around a word to make it bold is two [?]{.fitb answer="asterisks|stars|**"}.
(Type the word, or the symbol.)
